summary_html: CPS **accepts** a report for **investigation/assessment**. CAPTA sets the floor for investigation procedures; CFSR evaluates timeliness, safety, and decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — investigation standards tied to funding  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — timeliness & response conformity indicators

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court reversed the Superior Court, holding that an order compelling a parent to admit child-welfare workers into the home requires probable cause evaluated under ordinary search-and-seizure principles, and that a single stale, uncorroborated anonymous report did not supply it.
key_cases.relevance: Defines what the agency must show once it accepts a report and seeks court-backed access to the family.
key_cases.quote: We expressly hold that there is no "social worker exception" to compliance with constitutional limitations on an entry into a home without consent or exigent circumstances.

key_cases.case_name: Croft v. Westmoreland County Children & Youth Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
key_cases.holding: Reversing summary judgment for the caseworker, the court held that forcing a father from his home on the basis of an uncorroborated anonymous tip violated the family's substantive due process rights because the caseworker lacked objectively reasonable grounds to suspect abuse.
key_cases.relevance: Investigation may proceed on a tip, but coercive measures may not without objective corroboration.
key_cases.quote: we hold that she lacked objectively reasonable grounds to believe the child had been sexually abused or was in imminent danger of sexual abuse

key_cases.case_name: Good v. Dauphin County Social Services for Children & Youth
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court reversed summary judgment on qualified immunity, holding that on the mother's version of the facts a caseworker and police officer entered the home and strip-searched the child without valid consent, a warrant, or exigent circumstances, violating clearly established law.
key_cases.relevance: Sets the constitutional constraints on investigative techniques once a report is accepted.
key_cases.quote: under these circumstances a reasonable law enforcement officer could not have believed Ms. Good had given legally effective consent to either the entry or the subsequent strip search

key_cases.case_name: In re Petition to Compel Cooperation with Child Abuse Investigation
key_cases.holding: Vacating the order compelling parents to admit caseworkers, the court held that the CPSL and its mandatory home-visit regulation are subject to the Fourth Amendment and Article I, Section 8, so a petition to compel must allege facts amounting to probable cause, which a bare ChildLine referral of possible medical neglect did not.
key_cases.relevance: Defines what a county agency must plead once it accepts a report and seeks judicial compulsion of the family's cooperation.
key_cases.quote: if a home visit is refused and C & Y is unable to determine whether conditions in the home present a risk to the child, it must petition the court

state_agency.name: Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, Office of Children, Youth, and Families

timeline_requirements.deadline: 60 days in all cases; reasons for delay must be recorded if not completed within 30 days
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Investigation commenced by the county agency
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: The particular reasons for delay past 30 days must be described in the child protective service record and made available to the department to determine whether the county agency strictly followed 23 Pa.C.S. Ch. 63 and whether it is subject to action under 23 Pa.C.S. § 6343

timeline_requirements.deadline: 90 days to request an administrative review by, or appeal and request a hearing before, the secretary to amend or expunge an indicated report; the department sends notice of the secretary's decision within 60 days of a request for administrative review
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Notice to a person named as perpetrator, or to a school employee named, of the status of the indicated report
